Frontier models turn recurring operations in the traces into typed primitives and rules, and search assembles them using reference actions and training-task checks. A small frozen model executes the primitives, with deterministic verifiers checking their outputs. The resulting program guides a student's reasoning or checks its proposed actions. We evaluate the same program across students on $\tau^2$-Bench Retail and Telecom and LiveMCPBench, using synthetic training tasks and unseen benchmark test tasks. On Telecom, PLVR raises an 8B model's success rate from 43.0% to 91.2%, while larger students reach up to 94.4%, compared with 57.9% for the best baseline. On Retail and LiveMCPBench, PLVR is competitive with the best baselines, although tool search remains more dependent on the student model. These results support program learning as a way to transfer expert procedures across frozen models, trading additional inference computation for more reliable tool use.

articles.title: Beyond the Trial-and-Error Loop: Hybrid Projection and Automated Tuning for Distributed Training
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.19423v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Configuring distributed LLM training across hundreds of GPUs requires jointly optimizing tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism alongside micro-batch size, recomputation, sharding, and overlap, a combinatorial space where memory legality can hinge on a single byte of activation accounting. Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.

articles.title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.25096v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. RetailRAG consistently outperforms existing agentic RAG baselines across all evaluation axes, serving as a strong reference system for assessing LLM agents on retail workflows. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/DISL-Lab/RetailBridge.

articles.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.26185v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

articles.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.32477v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents. The project repository is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauProphet.

articles.title: IRON-Meme: A Benchmark for Structured Understanding of Identities and Roles in Online Meme Narratives
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.33097v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: As polarization grows on social media, understanding how political memes shape online narratives has become increasingly important. Previous research has relied on either qualitative frameworks that are hard to scale or computational methods that lack theoretical grounding. Both approaches treat narrative categories in isolation and focus exclusively on moral portrayals of identity. To address these limitations, we introduce a framework grounded in social science theories, encompassing three categories: social identities (such as gender, politics, and ethnicity), viewpoints (ingroup and outgroup perspectives), and narrative roles (moral character, intelligence, appearance, and power). Building on this framework, we present IRON-Meme, a human-annotated benchmark comprising 1,110 political memes across substantially more templates than existing benchmarks. Our analysis of IRON-Meme shows that most memes assign derogatory roles and that identities, roles, and templates are systematically interconnected. Evaluation of nine vision-language models indicates that frontier-scale and reasoning models achieve the highest performance, while accuracy on social identities and narrative roles decreases for less frequent labels. Incorporating template background knowledge does not enhance narrative role classification, suggesting that meme interpretation relies on how memes are adapted for specific communicative purposes. We make IRON-Meme and our code publicly available.

articles.title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care
articles.summary:
arXiv:2610.35847v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show growing promise in specialty medicine, yet existing evaluations largely focus on isolated clinical encounters rather than assessing the distinct clinical responsibilities along longitudinal care pathways. We introduce NPC-RubricBench, a phase-aware benchmark for evaluating multistage clinical reasoning across the cancer care continuum, using nasopharyngeal carcinoma as a defined disease context. Curated from real-world records of 405 patients at two cancer centers, it comprises 941 evaluation units across six sequential care stages, from work-up through follow-up, and 17,688 patient-specific criteria across five dimensions. Each assessment is restricted to clinical evidence available at the corresponding decision point. Across 30 general-purpose and medical LLMs, we find strong diagnostic scores did not ensure reliable downstream care. Decision Quality ranged from 56.8 to 94.7 in diagnosis on a 0-100 scale, but dropped to 8.9-56.0 in staging and spanned 32.4-94.2 in treatment. Crucially, failure modes differed across phases: explicit decision errors predominated in anatomical staging (48.2%), whereas decision omissions were more frequent during initial work-up (33.4%) and post-treatment follow-up (30.4%). Varying query granularity revealed a trade-off between decision quality and other clinical requirements. Broad open-ended requests reduced decision quality across all 30 models, whereas more detailed, checklist-like prompts improved decision quality but were accompanied by lower evidence faithfulness and safety adherence. These findings highlight the need to assess clinical reliability against the distinct clinical requirements of each phase along the longitudinal care pathway. Finally, NPC-RubricBench informs the design of stage-aware clinical guardrails and offers a reusable blueprint for evaluating LLMs across other cancers and chronic diseases.

articles.title: Early Stopping in Large Reasoning Models: A Survey and Empirical Audit of Efficiency and Reliability
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.00166v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large reasoning models can improve accuracy by generating longer reasoning traces, but some of this computation may be unnecessary. Early-stopping methods aim to stop once enough reasoning is available to answer. Evaluating these methods requires accounting for the cost of deciding when to stop and the reliability of the resulting answer. We evaluate different methods across five reasoning models on mathematical and scientific reasoning, code generation, and factuality tasks by using a shared rollout replay protocol. We introduce Target-Integrated Token Efficiency (TITE) to measure efficiency relative to the oracle across accuracy targets. We also examine correctness at later exit positions, transfer across models and tasks, post-stop reasoning continuation, and retained justification quality. In our experiments, correctness can decrease at later positions beyond what the fitted decoding-noise model predicts. Reliability checks also reveal continued reasoning after forced termination and weaker supporting reasoning in some correct early-stopping outputs. The implementation can be found in https://github.com/hung20gg/audit-early-stopping.

articles.title: Data-Scarce, Multi-Granular, Multimodal: Benchmark Design for Biosynthetic Gene Clusters
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.02275v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are co-located genes that encode the biosynthesis of specialized metabolites, an important source of antibiotics, anticancer agents, immunosuppressants, and agricultural bioactives. Deep learning, particularly self-supervised foundation models, has spurred interest in BGC sequence modeling, but evaluation has lagged behind: existing benchmarks often rely on coarse classification over small curated datasets, providing limited discrimination among models and insight into downstream utility. We propose a benchmark-design framework in which an informative benchmark should be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks under different levels of generalization. We instantiate this framework as BGC-Bench, which derives five tasks from MIBiG, ranging from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, includes an active-learning setting for label-scarce discovery, and is easily extensible to new tasks and encoders. BGCs further provide a shared testbed across granularities and modalities: BGC-Bench compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid, or Pfam-domain sequences, including compositional baselines for each input type, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval. No single representation dominates: the best granularity depends on the biological scale of the task, and pretrained encoders do not consistently outperform other representations across tasks and splits. Active-learning experiments show that most tasks remain data-limited, encoder rankings change with labeling budget, and acquisition strategies yield modest gains. These results show that BGC model evaluation requires task-diverse, shift-aware benchmarks, and the framework can be generalized to benchmark design beyond BGCs.

articles.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.03233v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.

articles.title: LOLPlay: Benchmarking Real-Time Visual Agents in League of Legends
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.03685v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Visual agents need to coordinate reasoning and action while their environment evolves during inference. We introduce LOLPlay, a benchmark in native League of Legends with 36 champion-specific tasks spanning resource management, combat, cooperation, and objectives. Agents interact through screenshots and mouse-keyboard actions; automated initialization and 82 executable subgoal checks distinguish partial progress from completion. Across 324 task evaluations of three models at three reasoning-effort settings, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate of 25.0% at low and medium effort, and the highest subgoal success rate of 40.3% at medium effort. However, high effort improves neither metric over low effort for any model. For Astra, longer requests leave fewer interaction rounds, suggesting a cost to additional reasoning in real-time control. Trajectories reveal incomplete subgoal composition and actions executing after the observed scene changes, motivating agents that combine visual reasoning with timely action.

articles.title: SafeOrchestrate: Runtime Checked Intent-Driven Orchestration for Cyber-Physical Systems
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.09364v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern cyber physical systems (CPS) integrate heterogeneous sensors, actuators, controllers, and services, composed at runtime rather than at design time. Orchestrating such systems through natural language (NL) is attractive, but unconstrained large language model (LLM) tool use is risky because actions must respect device capabilities, runtime state, and safety constraints. We present Safe Orchestrate, a reference architecture for runtime checked, intent driven CPS orchestration. Given an NL intent, it derives atomic goals, generates a runtime checkable specification for each, grounds the specifications to device affordances, and verifies every candidate action against runtime state and safety constraints before execution. In a Web of Things (WoT) instantiation, the architecture produces Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) style specifications from the NL intent, grounds them to Thing Description (TD) affordances exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and checks candidate actions against satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) backed guardrails. We evaluate this instantiation on simulated smart home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks against a direct LLM to MCP baseline. Safe Orchestrate maintains 100% required action accuracy on every task and 100% MCP Execution Similarity (MCP ES) on all but one, where MCP ES is 92%. By contrast, the baseline degrades on multi device, event triggered, and ordered tasks, with MCP ES falling to 13%. These results suggest that combining LLM based specification generation with role aware grounding and runtime constraint checking improves reliability for open CPS orchestration without enriched TD annotations or planning domain expertise.

articles.title: Don't Blame The Preferences: Examining The Emergence of Sycophancy in LLM Training
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.10045v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI sycophancy, the tendency of large language models (LLMs) to flatter users and affirm their beliefs, can undermine accuracy and contribute to misinformation, dependence, and overconfidence. Although prior work has benchmarked sycophancy in released models and proposed mitigations, its origins during training remain poorly understood. Preference alignment methods such as RLHF and DPO are often blamed, but their effects are rarely compared with earlier training stages. We investigate sycophancy across the training pipelines of three model families and three benchmarks. We find that sycophancy is largely established by the end of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), rather than introduced by preference alignment. Across all nine model benchmark combinations, SFT checkpoints attain at least 92% of preference aligned models' sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final models' scores; on average, they are about as sycophantic as final models. Preference alignment increases sycophancy in only four of nine cases, by an average of 4.2 percentage points when it does. To probe the underlying causes, we isolate model representations associated with sycophancy using mechanistic interpretability and measure their activation on training datasets from each stage. SFT datasets show roughly the same average activation as other training data but contribute substantially more examples, and the highest-scoring individual datasets all come from SFT. Our findings suggest that addressing sycophancy requires interventions throughout the training pipeline, particularly in data selection and augmentation for pre-training and SFT.

articles.title: BunshinRL: Whole-Workspace Forking for Agentic Reinforcement Learning Rollouts
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.10453v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.

articles.title: Characterizing Scanpath Decoding Pipelines with Perturbation Profiles
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.11632v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: When a scanpath descriptor supports a classification, it is rarely clear what the classification rests on. We propose perturbation profiles. Five transformations each target one stated property of every scanpath (fixation order, the coupling of durations to positions, the duration distribution, orientation and handedness, and fine spatial structure) while preserving a listed set of invariants. The classifier is refit, and the change in participant-held-out AUC is the pipeline's sensitivity to that property. Intervals come from a participant bootstrap that refits the classifier; in simulations they were conservative (99.7% coverage; standard errors about 1.8 times the empirical spread). We profiled nine descriptors on thirteen binary problems from three public datasets, with a within-fold AUC and class-balanced folds and a stated rule for which sensitivities to interpret. Of 565 intervals, 95 excluded zero; 80 were robust to the pooled AUC, 20 fold partitions and longer runs (36 of them within +/-0.05 AUC), and 45 also held with boosted trees. Most came from GazeBase (322 participants). Permuting fixation order raised the AUC of a descriptor based on mean saccade amplitude, because permuted amplitude has as its expectation the mean pairwise distance, a measure of spread. A "comprehension" contrast pooled over two programs was a contrast between their layouts: it vanished among trials of the same program, and synthetic gaze drawn from the layout alone reproduced the program contrast beneath it. For native versus non-native readers, spatial jitter at the scale of text lines reduced recurrence's discrimination. A Python package is released.

articles.title: AutoQS: Automated Quantization Strategy Design with Large Language Models
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.11975v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation. This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs. AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations. An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals. Periodic actual quantization complements these proxy evaluations with measured quality and checkpoint storage, providing feedback for further search within the evaluation budget. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ by 0.70 and 1.12 percentage points, respectively, at four-bit weight precision.

articles.title: Evaluating AI Agents for Industrial-Level Chip Floorplanning: A Framework and Empirical Study
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.12048v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Floorplanning is an early step in turning a logical circuit into a physical chip: it positions large circuit modules and constrains the space available for subsequent logic placement and wiring. These decisions affect congestion and timing, but their physical consequences emerge through downstream implementation. For AI agents, the task requires translating engineering constraints into spatial decisions whose quality cannot be judged by successful tool execution alone. We present an evaluation framework that connects submitted layouts to a prescribed downstream implementation flow, checks geometric validity, measures physical quality, and reports resource use. On one industrial design whose 99 macros occupy approximately 71\% of a fixed L-shaped layout region, we compare our specialized system Nova-SI with general-purpose engineering agents and agents restricted to file access, obtaining complete physical measurements for 39 layout outputs. Under our 0--100 composite quality score, Nova-SI achieves a mean of 57.97 without online feedback from the prescribed power-grid and placement evaluation, compared with 31.17 for the strongest measured general-purpose configuration, GPT-6 Astra. The difference is supported by raw congestion and timing measurements and persists across scoring-sensitivity checks. Layout-level analysis further shows that similar global utilization can conceal substantially different local congestion. Together, the protocol and case study assess agents through the physical consequences of their delivered layouts and provide evidence about system performance on this industrial instance.

articles.title: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.12109v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.

articles.title: DForkTree: Accelerating Speculative Decoding with Fork-Aware Block Diffusion Draft Trees
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.12356v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up language models by having a lightweight drafter propose future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash predict an entire block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds draft trees directly from their per-position distributions. Each distribution implicitly assumes that the drafter's own greedy continuation is accepted, whereas a draft tree improves over a chain only on branches that leave this greedy path. Once a path forks, the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its top candidates often miss the true token. Re-running the drafter from the fork token largely restores its accuracy, showing that the errors stem from conditioning on an outdated prefix rather than from limited model capacity. In this paper, we introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens. It adjusts the drafter's scores with pointwise mutual information from target-generated n-grams, weighted more heavily after a fork, and a layer-wise GPU search recovers the exact optimal tree under these scores. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, by up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.

articles.title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.12865v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing violations of explicitly stated contextual requirements, even when reward accurately measures useful work. We study this reward-driven misalignment through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant completion is feasible but executable violations earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics supports scalable environment construction and compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. We observe both amplification of existing violations and the emergence of violations on tasks where none were observed before training. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1% to 89.1% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

articles.title: Reliability of Claude Code as an Agentic AI Grading System for Handwritten University Exams
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.13217v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This study examines the reliability of Claude Code, an agentic deployment of the Claude Opus 4.6 large language model, as a grading system for handwritten university exams. Four research questions addressed agreement with expert human grading on total scores (RQ1), agreement across five question types from multiple choice to evaluative judgement (RQ2), consistency across two independent grading sessions one week apart (RQ3), and the accuracy of AI-generated feedback (RQ4). Claude Code graded the 20-mark mid-term papers of 60 consenting students in a Saudi computer graphics course in a single agentic session, guided by three rubric files. Reliability was estimated on disjoint samples: 20 papers for RQ1, RQ2 and RQ4, and 15 papers for RQ3. Analyses used Pearson correlation, mean absolute error, Bland-Altman analysis, weighted Cohen kappa, intraclass correlation, and a four-category coding scheme separating diagnostic from confirmation feedback. The author, as the sole subject-matter expert for the course, provided the human benchmark, so the design assesses agreement with a domain-expert reference rather than inter-rater reliability. AI grading agreed strongly with human grading on totals (r = 0.97; MAE = 0.85 marks) with a small but significant AI-positive bias of 0.68 marks, showed excellent test-retest consistency (ICC = 0.96), and produced accurate feedback (92.8% diagnostic; 97.8% confirmation). Drawing items were the outlier on three of four measures. Three failure modes recurred: keyword matching without conceptual depth, selection-state ambiguity on corrected multiple-choice answers, and region-of-attention drift on hand-drawn diagrams. The findings suggest that AI grading at this capability level can assist instructors on objective and short-form items under structural safeguards but is not yet ready to replace instructor judgement at boundary cases or on drawing items.

articles.title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
articles.summary:
arXiv:2611.13651v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.

articles.title: Approximate and Weighted Data Reconstruction Attack in Federated Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2308.06822v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning paradigm that enables multiple clients to collaborate on building a machine learning model without sharing their private data. Although FL is considered privacy-preserved by design, recent data reconstruction attacks demonstrate that an attacker can recover clients' training data based on the parameters shared in FL. However, most existing methods fail to attack the most widely used horizontal Federated Averaging (FedAvg) scenario, where clients share model parameters after multiple local training steps. To tackle this issue, we propose an interpolation-based approximation method, which makes attacking FedAvg scenarios feasible by generating the intermediate model updates of the clients' local training processes. Then, we design a layer-wise weighted loss function to improve the data quality of reconstruction. We assign different weights to model updates in different layers concerning the neural network structure, with the weights tuned by Bayesian optimization. Finally, experimental results validate the superiority of our proposed approximate and weighted attack (AWA) method over the other state-of-the-art methods, as demonstrated by the substantial improvement in different evaluation metrics for image data reconstructions. The source code is available at https://github.com/DCN-FAU-AvH/FL-AWA-attack.

articles.title: A hybrid FEM-PINN method for time-dependent partial differential equations
articles.summary:
arXiv:2409.02810v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this work, we present a hybrid numerical method for solving evolution partial differential equations (PDEs) by merging the time finite element method with deep neural networks. In contrast to the conventional deep learning-based formulation where the neural network is defined on a spatiotemporal domain, our methodology utilizes finite element basis functions in the time direction where the space-dependent coefficients are defined as the output of a neural network. We then apply the Galerkin or collocation projection in the time direction to obtain a system of PDEs for the space-dependent coefficients which is approximated in the framework of PINN. The advantages of such a hybrid formulation are twofold: statistical errors are avoided for the integral in the time direction, and the neural network's output can be regarded as a set of reduced spatial basis functions. To further alleviate the difficulties from high dimensionality and low regularity, we have developed an adaptive sampling strategy that refines the training set. More specifically, we use an explicit density model to approximate the distribution induced by the PDE residual and then augment the training set with new time-dependent random samples given by the learned density model. The effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method have been demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments.

articles.title: FACE: Few-shot Adapter with Cross-view Fusion for Cross-subject EEG Emotion Recognition
articles.summary:
arXiv:2503.18998v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is challenged by significant inter-subject variability and intricately entangled intra-subject variability. Existing works have primarily addressed these challenges through domain adaptation or generalization strategies. However, they typically require extensive target subject data or demonstrate limited generalization performance to unseen subjects. Recent few-shot learning paradigms attempt to address these limitations but often encounter catastrophic overfitting during subject-specific adaptation with limited samples. This article introduces the few-shot adapter with a cross-view fusion method called FACE for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition, which leverages dynamic cross-view fusion and effective subject-specific adaptation. Specifically, FACE incorporates a cross-view fusion module that dynamically integrates global brain connectivity with localized patterns via subject-specific fusion weights to provide complementary emotional information. Moreover, the few-shot adapter module is proposed to enable rapid adaptation for unseen subjects while reducing overfitting by enhancing adapter structures with meta-learning. Experimental results on three public EEG emotion recognition benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of FACE under few-shot cross-subject evaluation.

articles.title: Shannon observables: A scalable approach to information decomposition
articles.summary:
arXiv:2504.15779v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Distributed systems, such as biological and artificial neural networks, process information via complex interactions engaging multiple subsystems, resulting in high-order structure of the information within the system with distinct properties across scales. Investigating how these systems process information remains challenging due to difficulties in defining appropriate multivariate metrics and ensuring their scalability to large systems. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework based on what we call "Shannon observables": quantities that capture essential properties of high-order information processing, yet can be computed directly from Shannon entropies and scale efficiently to large systems. Our theoretical results demonstrate how Shannon observables can be used to resolve long-standing ambiguities regarding the interpretation of widely used multivariate information-theoretic measures. On the practical side, we demonstrate the framework's versatility across several domains. An analytical study of error-correcting codes shows how Shannon observables trace out distinct encoding regimes as channel noise varies; analyses of deep classifiers and convolutional autoencoders reveal characteristic information-processing signatures across layers and over training; and applied to magnetoencephalography recordings from the human brain, the framework yields a cortical atlas exposing pronounced regional structure in directed information transfer. Overall, our framework resolves fundamental limitations in analysing high-order information phenomena and offers broad opportunities for theoretical developments and empirical analyses.

articles.title: Silent Neuron Theory and Plasticity Preservation for Deep Reinforcement Learning in Adaptive Video Streaming
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.01584v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Adaptive video streaming optimizes Quality of Experience (QoE) metrics by selecting appropriate bitrates according to varying network bandwidth and user demands. In practice, however, real-world network bandwidth often exhibits heterogeneity relative to training environments. Current methods predominantly tackle this problem through learning-based approaches designed to improve generalization performance. Our systematic investigation reveals a critical limitation: neural networks suffer from plasticity loss, significantly impeding their ability to adapt to heterogeneous network conditions. Through theoretical analysis of neural propagation mechanisms, we demonstrate that existing dormant neuron metrics inadequately characterize neural plasticity loss. To address this limitation, we have developed the Silent Neuron theory, which provides a more comprehensive framework for understanding plasticity degradation. Based on these theoretical insights, we propose the Reset Silent Neuron (ReSiN), which preserves neural plasticity through strategic neuron resets guided by both forward and backward propagation states. Moreover, we establish a tighter performance bound for ReSiN under non-stationary network conditions. In our implementation of an adaptive video streaming system, ReSiN shows substantial gains under non-stationary conditions in which the available bandwidth alternates between high and low regimes, improving the QoE by 178%, and it remains beneficial under stationary real-world traces, where it improves the QoE by 1.6%. Code will be available: https://tinyzqh.github.io/ReSiN/

articles.title: OPA-Pack: Object-Property-Aware Robotic Bin Packing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2505.13339v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Robotic bin packing is a fundamental manipulation problem with broad applications in e-commerce and warehouse automation. However, existing methods primarily focus on object geometry to optimize packing compactness without explicitly modeling object properties such as fragility, edibility, and chemical compatibility that humans typically consider during packing. This paper presents OPA-Pack (Object-Property-Aware Packing), a framework that incorporates object-property information into robotic bin-packing planning. The framework includes an object property recognition scheme based on retrieval-augmented generation and chain-of-thought reasoning to establish a dataset with object property annotations for 1,032 everyday objects. The framework further incorporates OPA-Net, which encodes candidate-object properties via a property embedding layer and represents the container state using fragility and avoidance heightmaps. We design a reward function and adopt a deep Q-learning scheme to train OPA-Net. Experimental results show that OPA-Pack improves avoidance accuracy from 52.3% to 95.0%, reduces load on fragile objects by 29.4%, and achieves a packing compactness of 0.413, compared with 0.420 for the baseline. In addition, we evaluate OPA-Pack on a physical platform using 70 packing sequences sampled from 100 scanned real-world objects. Results show that OPA-Pack outperforms the baseline and other packing heuristics in reducing the number of closely packed incompatible object pairs and the number of compressed fragile objects while preserving packing compactness.

articles.title: Specification-based Security Evaluation of Real-World Agents Tool-Calling under Long-Horizon Context Tasks
articles.summary:
arXiv:2506.15253v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon unattended scenarios, security evaluation of them before deployment becomes increasingly essential and challenging. Existing evaluation methods mainly follow the paradigms of LLM-as-a-Judge or Agent-as-a-Judge. However, such judges are themselves often vulnerable to hallucination and can even be affected by perturbations. Furthermore, because capturing full environment states at every step is often prohibitively expensive in open-ended environments, existing evaluations typically rely on textual logs and the final environment state. As a result, they may miss transient violations that are overwritten before the trajectory ends or never reflected in textual logs. We present RAS-Eval, a specification-based security evaluation framework for LLM agents. RAS-Eval uniformly expresses utility and security objectives as Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications over tool-call trajectories and dynamic environment observations, and verifies them with an off-the-shelf model checker. This design addresses both limitations above. First, unlike LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge, RAS-Eval derives deterministic verdicts from formally defined properties, eliminating evaluator-side uncertainty and remaining reliable even for long-horizon trajectories. Second, RAS-Eval observes exactly the states on which the verdict depends, making it affordable to monitor the environment throughout execution and detect transient violations that leave little trace in the logs or final environment state. Moreover, we design a multi-agent-based dataset construction pipeline. Using it, we construct a benchmark (https://github.com/lanzer-tree/RAS-Eval) of 200 normal tasks and 800 attack tasks spanning four attack surfaces: indirect prompt injection, tool poisoning, skill code injection, and tool code injection.

articles.title: Lilith: Developmental Modular LLMs with Chemical Signaling
articles.summary:
arXiv:2507.04575v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Current paradigms in Artificial Intelligence rely on layers of feedforward networks which model brain activity at the neuronal level. We conjecture that expanding to the level of multiple brain regions with chemical signaling may be a productive step toward understanding the emergence of consciousness. We propose LILITH, a novel architecture that combines developmental training of modular language models with brain-inspired token-based communication protocols, mirroring chemical signaling in the brain. Our approach models distinct brain regions as specialized LLM modules including thinking, memory, sensory, and regulatory components that communicate through emergent token-based signaling protocols analogous to neurotransmitter networks. Unlike traditional pre-trained systems, LILITH would employ developmental training where untrained LLM architectures learn through simulated life experiences, developing communication pathways and cognitive abilities through environmental interaction and evolutionary optimization. This framework would enable direct empirical investigation of consciousness emergence using Integrated Information Theory metrics while providing unprecedented insight into inter-module signaling patterns during development. By optimizing for consciousness emergence rather than task performance, LILITH could provide insight into different emergent phenomena at multiple levels of neural correlates, contrasting neuronal-level processing with multi-region coordination dynamics. The goal of this paper is to put the idea forward while recognizing the substantial challenges in implementing such a system.

articles.title: Re-evaluating Heart Rate Variability Biomarkers for Glucose Sensing: The Impact of Age Normalisation and Subject-Independent Validation
articles.summary:
arXiv:2508.11682v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Heart rate variability (HRV) from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals may indicate glycemic status, but prior studies often combine distinct glucose targets and use validation strategies vulnerable to data leakage. Since HRV declines with age, aging may be confounded with diabetes-related autonomic dysfunction. We tested whether age-dependent HRV normalisation improves glycemic estimation. We analysed ECG features from 43 male patients with type 2 diabetes. Outcomes were glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c; n=29) and fasting blood glucose (FBG; n=38). We used leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, with feature selection and standardisation within each training fold. We compared 20 machine-learning algorithms, six age-adjustment methods, and 20 normalisation parameter combinations. Validation included 500 permutations and bootstrap confidence intervals. Extra Trees regression performed best: R2=0.222 (r=0.476, p=0.009) for HbA1c and R2=0.086 (r=0.344, p=0.034) for FBG. Mean absolute errors were 1.18 percentage points and 2.27 mmol/L, respectively. Permutation testing supported both associations (p=0.002). Contrary to our hypothesis, no age-adjustment method or parameter combination improved performance. Tree ensembles retained positive performance under strict validation, whereas linear models had negative R2 values; neural networks performed poorly. Strict within-fold preprocessing materially changed model performance and revealed potential inflation from conventional validation. Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were [0.13, 0.82] for HbA1c R2 and [0.10, 0.72] for FBG R2. Although findings support HRV-glycemic associations, performance remains insufficient for standalone clinical use. The study highlights the importance of separating glycemic targets, subject-independent validation, within-fold preprocessing, and comprehensive baselines in non-invasive glycemic monitoring research.

articles.title: FoMEMO: Towards Foundation Models for Expensive Multi-objective Optimization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2509.03244v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Expensive multi-objective optimization is a prevalent and crucial concern in many real-world scenarios, where sample-efficiency is vital due to the limited evaluations to recover the true Pareto front for decision making. Existing works either involve repeatedly fitting Gaussian process surrogates from scratch for each newly encountered problem, or rely on computationally demanding hypervolume-oriented policy learning for amortized optimization, making it challenging to achieve scalable pre-training and efficient yet robust adaptation for diverse emerging real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose FoMEMO (Foundation Models for Expensive Multi-objective Optimization), which adopts a decomposition-based training paradigm that converts multi-objective optimization into preference-wise aggregated posterior learning tasks, enabling scalable pre-training on hundreds of millions of diverse synthetic datasets without relying on extensive real-world domain experiments. At test time, given observed trajectories from unseen problems and user preferences, the foundation model performs in-context posterior prediction and optimizes the derived acquisition functions for efficient candidate generation, achieving strong generalization and optimization performance without any subsequent model training or updates.

articles.title: Catch-Only-One: Non-Transferable Examples for Model-Specific Authorization
articles.summary:
arXiv:2510.10982v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Recent AI regulations increasingly emphasize the need for mechanisms that preserve the utility of data for AI innovation while preventing misuse, particularly by enforcing purpose limitation in downstream AI applications. In practice, enforcing this principle remains challenging, as released data can be trivially fed into arbitrary models beyond its declared intent. Existing approaches attempt to mitigate this risk by either perturbing data or retraining models to limit unintended use. These strategies, however, offer no protection against inference by unknown or externally trained models, or fundamentally rely on control over the training or deployment. In this work, we introduce non-transferable examples (NTEs), recoded data that act as a task-level "ciphertext" decodable only by a designated model. Whereas adversarial examples exploit directions of high model sensitivity, NTEs leverage the complementary insensitive subspace. We propose a training-free, data-agnostic method that recodes data within a model-specific low-sensitivity subspace, preserving outputs for the authorized model while degrading unauthorized ones through subspace misalignment. We establish formal bounds certifying authorized-model fidelity and showing that unauthorized degradation scales with measurable spectral misalignment between models. Empirically, NTEs preserve performance across diverse vision backbones and state-of-the-art vision-language models under common preprocessing, while unauthorized models collapse even under adaptive reconstruction attacks. These results establish NTEs as a practical means to preserve intended data utility while preventing unauthorized exploitation. Our project is available at https://trusted-system-lab.github.io/model-specificity.

articles.title: DAISY: Fault-Guided Assertion Inference for Dafny
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.00125v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Formal verification with Dafny provides strong correctness guarantees, but verification failures often require users to determine where helper assertions are needed and to manually write the assertions necessary for verification to succeed. This proof-engineering burden is difficult, time-consuming, and a barrier to the adoption of verification-aware languages.
  We present DAISY (Dafny Assertion Inference SYstem), a tool for fault-guided assertion inference in Dafny.
  Given a Dafny program and a target method, DAISY localizes likely assertion sites using verifier diagnostics, LLM-based localization, or their combination. It then annotates the program with assertion placeholders, retrieves relevant in-context examples, generates candidate assertions with an LLM, and validates candidates by running the Dafny verifier.
  To evaluate DAISY, we extend DafnyBench with verification-failing variants created by removing helper assertions from verified programs. The resulting benchmark distinguishes between programs with one missing assertion, two missing assertions, and all assertions removed, allowing us to evaluate DAISY on increasingly difficult proof failures. On this benchmark, DAISY verifies 86\% of programs with a single missing assertion and 36\% of programs with two missing assertions. These results show that fault-guided LLM assertion inference can repair many Dafny verification failures. They also show that successful repairs often differ from the original assertions, reducing proof-engineering effort without reconstructing the original proof.

articles.title: Individualized Algorithmic Advice as a Strategic Signal on Competitive Markets
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.09454v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: As algorithms increasingly mediate competitive decision-making, their influence extends beyond individual outcomes to shaping strategic market dynamics. In our experiment, we examined how algorithmic advice affects human behavior in a classic economic game with a unique, non-collusive, and analytically traceable equilibrium. Participants (N = 129) played a Cournot quantity competition with equilibrium-aligned or strategically biased algorithmic recommendations. While individualized equilibrium advice supported stable convergence, collusively downward-biased advice led to sustained underproduction and supracompetitive profits - hallmarks of tacit collusion. Participants' quantities converged faster and more consistently toward individualized than collective equilibrium advice, potentially due to an objective quality advantage or greater perceived ownership of the former. These findings demonstrate that algorithmic advice can function as a strategic signal, shaping coordination even without explicit communication. The results echo real-world concerns about algorithmic collusion and underscore the need for careful design and oversight of algorithmic decision-support systems in competitive environments.

articles.title: LLM4SCREENLIT: Recommendations on assessing the performance of large language models for screening literature in systematic reviews
articles.summary:
arXiv:2511.12635v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Context: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen literature for systematic reviews (SRs), but the standard confusion-matrix metrics used to evaluate them can mislead under the imbalanced, cost-asymmetric conditions of screening.
  Objective: We develop and justify LLM4SCREENLIT-practical recommendations for researchers conducting LLM-screening evaluations and for editors and reviewers assessing such studies-differentiated by study type (retrospective benchmarking vs deployment for a specific SR).
  Method: Using Delgado-Chaves et al. (2025), an 18-LLM benchmark across three biomedical SRs, as a motivating example, we reviewed 28 additional papers and extracted their reported metrics. We propose a Weighted Matthews Correlation Coefficient (WMCC) that integrates MCC's chance-correction with asymmetric misclassification costs, and validated it on three software-engineering (SE) reanalyses, the largest covering 9 LLMs x 24 SE secondary studies (34,528 articles).
  Results: Across the 29 papers, only 10% reported MCC, only 24% reported full confusion matrices, and none of the five papers claiming workload savings priced false-negative cost. In the largest SE reanalysis, MCC and WMCC disagree on the best LLM in 55% of evaluable studies; in the most striking 9,695-article SE study, the Accuracy-best LLM loses 63.3% of relevant evidence (Lost Evidence), the MCC-best 43.9%, but the WMCC-best only 5.8%. Sensitivity analysis (median crossover at w~=2.7, all <7) supports w=10 as a conservative default.
  Conclusions: SR-screening evaluations should prioritize Lost Evidence and use cost-sensitive WMCC alongside MCC for ranking. Reporting must include the full confusion matrix and treat unclassifiable outputs as positives requiring human review. Designs should be leakage-aware, with non-LLM baselines when the study aims to inform SR practice and labels are available.

articles.title: CUDA-L2: Surpassing cuBLAS Performance for Matrix Multiplication through Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.02551v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this paper, we propose CUDA-L2, a system that combines large language models (LLMs) and reinforcement learning (RL) to automatically optimize Half-precision General Matrix Multiply (HGEMM) CUDA kernels. Using CUDA execution speed as the RL reward, CUDA-L2 automatically optimizes HGEMM kernels across 1,000 configurations. CUDA-L2 systematically outperforms major matmul baselines to date, from the widely-used torch.matmul to state-of-the-art Nvidia's closed-source libraries, i.e., cuBLAS, cuBLASLt. In offline mode, where kernels are executed consecutively without time intervals, CUDA-L2 yields +22.0% over torch.matmul on average; +19.2% over cuBLAS using the optimal layout configuration (normal-normal NN and transposed-normal TN); +16.8% over cuBLASLt-heuristic, which queries cuBLASLt library and selects the algorithm based on the heuristic's suggestion; and +11.4% over the most competitive cuBLASLt-AutoTuning model, which selects the fastest algorithm from up to 100 candidates from cuBLASLt's suggestions. In server mode, where kernels are executed at random intervals simulating real-time inference, the speedups further increase to +28.7%, +26.0%, +22.4%, and +15.9% for torch.matmul, cuBLAS, cuBLASLt-heuristic, and cuBLASLt-AutoTuning respectively. CUDA-L2 shows that even the most performance-critical, heavily-optimized kernels like HGEMM can be improved through LLM-guided RL automation by systematically exploring configuration spaces at scales impractical for humans. Project and code can be found at github.com/ornith-ai/CUDA-L2

articles.title: Towards Accurate UAV Image Perception: Guiding Vision-Language Models with Stronger Task Prompts
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.07302v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: UAV image perception with VLMs aims to identify and localize targets based on semantic and spatial task prompts. However, small, densely distributed objects and cluttered backgrounds hinder these tasks, particularly when concise prompts provide insufficient guidance. Although task-specific fine-tuning improves image-text alignment, it requires large-scale annotations and model-specific updates, increasing adaptation costs across models and tasks. To address this, we propose AerialVP, a task-adaptive, training-free agent that adapts VLMs through prompt enhancement rather than parameter optimization. AerialVP dynamically adapts its enhancement strategy to the original prompt's specificity, selectively incorporating image-derived semantics, spatial positions, and object relationships. These cues provide discriminative descriptions and spatial constraints, leveraging VLMs' pretrained alignment and reasoning capabilities to improve image-text alignment and reduce target ambiguity. Specifically, an LLM-based Task Engine coordinates modular tools for prompt analysis, visual information extraction, and prompt fusion. The enhanced prompt and original image are then provided to the unchanged backend VLM for prediction. This prompt-centric strategy enables training-free adaptation across diverse open-source and proprietary VLMs. For systematic evaluation, we introduce AerialSense, a unified benchmark covering Aerial Visual Grounding, Aerial Visual Reasoning, and Aerial Visual Question Answering across diverse UAV scenes and imaging conditions. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across all three tasks and evaluated VLMs. AerialVP also achieves competitive performance against LoRA-based instruction fine-tuning, validating prompt-centric adaptation. Our work is available at https://github.com/lostwolves/AerialVP.

articles.title: Extrapolation of Periodic Functions Using Binary Encoding of Continuous Numerical Values
articles.summary:
arXiv:2512.10817v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce Normalized Base-2 Encoding (NB2E) as a method for encoding continuous numerical values and demonstrate that, using this input encoding, vanilla multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) successfully extrapolate four periodic waveforms without prior knowledge of their functional form. We contrast this finding with fixed Fourier encoding, which extrapolates well when the number of signal cycles over the normalized domain is an even integer and loses coherence at most other values, whereas NB2E degrades gradually away from those values and, except near odd cycle counts, remains substantially more accurate. These findings are limited to a single MLP architecture trained on one synthetic, exactly periodic, one-dimensional signal at a time, with extrapolation extending only to the end of the normalized domain. We do not propose a mechanism for this phenomenon. Rather, we present empirical observations which merit further study.

articles.title: Will It Survive? Deciphering the Fate of AI Agent-Authored Code in Open Source
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.16809v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: AI coding agents such as GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex and Devin now open pull requests (PRs) that are merged into open-source projects. Industry reports suggest that AI-assisted code is revised or reverted soon after it is written, which raises the concern that agent code is "disposable". However, little is known about what happens to agent code after it is merged. Knowing how long this code survives, and why it is changed, can help maintainers decide how much review it needs. We performed a survival analysis of the 648,959 lines that 2,794 merged PRs added outside vendored and generated paths in 215 open-source repositories from the AIDev dataset, comparing agent-attributed and human code within the same repositories. Agent-attributed code is not modified sooner than human code. When each PR is weighted equally, agent-attributed lines are modified later (HR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.75, 0.93]). This difference comes from the supervised assistants, mainly Copilot and Codex (HR = 0.76). Code from Devin does not differ from human code over the whole period (HR = 0.95), but among PRs merged after mid-May 2025, code from both the supervised assistants and Devin is modified later. Without PR weighting, the difference is not statistically significant. When agent-attributed code is modified, the intent of the change is similar to that of human code (Cramer's V = 0.080). A file's size and recent changes predict whether agent-attributed code will be modified better than its code tokens do (AUC-ROC 0.78 vs. 0.70), and process features predict when it will be modified only weakly (Macro F1 of 0.31 against 0.25 for a random guess). Our findings suggest that agent code is not disposable, but whether it survives longer than human code depends on the agent, on when the code was merged and on how the comparison is computed.

articles.title: ART for Diffusion Sampling: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Timestep Scheduling
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.18681v4 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We consider time discretization for score-based diffusion models to generate samples from a learned reverse-time dynamic on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted grids can be suboptimal given a budget on the number of time steps. We introduce Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), which controls the clock speed of a reparameterized time variable to redistribute computation along the sampling trajectory while preserving the terminal time, with the objective of minimizing the aggregate Euler discretization error. We derive a randomized companion ART-RL that recasts ART as a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem with Gaussian policies, and prove a two-directional bridge between the two: the deterministic ART optimum lifts to an optimal Gaussian policy, and conversely any optimal Gaussian policy must recover the ART control through its mean. This bridge turns continuous-time actor--critic learning into a principled, rather than heuristic, route to the deterministic timestep optimum. Within the official EDM pipeline, ART-RL improves FID on CIFAR--10 across a wide range of budgets; after one-time offline training, the distilled deterministic schedule transfers without retraining to AFHQv2, FFHQ, and ImageNet at no extra inference cost.

articles.title: XFACTORS: Disentangled Information Bottleneck via Contrastive Supervision
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.21688v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Disentangled representation learning aims to map independent factors of variation to independent representation components. On one hand, purely unsupervised approaches have proven successful on fully disentangled synthetic data, but fail to recover semantic factors from real data without strong inductive biases. On the other hand, supervised approaches are unstable and hard to scale to large attribute sets because they rely on adversarial objectives or auxiliary classifiers.
  We introduce \textsc{XFactors}, a weakly-supervised VAE framework that disentangles and provides explicit control over a chosen set of factors. Building on the Disentangled Information Bottleneck perspective, we decompose the representation into a residual subspace $\mathcal{S}$ and factor-specific subspaces $\mathcal{T}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{T}_K$ and a residual subspace $\mathcal{S}$. Each target factor is encoded in its assigned $\mathcal{T}_i$ through contrastive supervision: an InfoNCE loss pulls together latents sharing the same factor value and pushes apart mismatched pairs. In parallel, KL regularization imposes a Gaussian structure on both $\mathcal{S}$ and the aggregated factor subspaces, organizing the geometry without additional supervision for non-targeted factors and avoiding adversarial training and classifiers.
  Across multiple datasets, with constant hyperparameters, \textsc{XFactors} achieves state-of-the-art disentanglement scores and yields consistent qualitative factor alignment in the corresponding subspaces, enabling controlled factor swapping via latent replacement. We further demonstrate that our method scales correctly with increasing latent capacity and evaluate it on the real-world dataset CelebA. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/ICML26-anon/XFactors}{github.com/ICML26-anon/XFactors}.

articles.title: VMonarch: Efficient Video Diffusion Transformers with Structured Attention
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.22275v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The quadratic complexity of the attention mechanism severely limits the context scalability of Video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). We find that the highly sparse spatio-temporal attention patterns exhibited in Video DiTs can be naturally represented by the Monarch matrix. It is a class of structured matrices with flexible sparsity, enabling sub-quadratic attention via an alternating minimization algorithm. Accordingly, we propose VMonarch, a novel attention mechanism for Video DiTs that enables efficient computation over the dynamic sparse patterns with structured Monarch matrices. First, we adapt spatio-temporal Monarch factorization to explicitly capture the intra-frame and inter-frame correlations of the video data. Second, we introduce a recomputation strategy to mitigate artifacts arising from instabilities during alternating minimization of Monarch matrices. Third, we propose a novel online entropy algorithm fused into FlashAttention, enabling fast Monarch matrix updates for long sequences. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VMonarch achieves comparable or superior generation quality to full attention on VBench after minimal tuning. It overcomes the attention bottleneck in Video DiTs, reduces attention FLOPs by a factor of 17.5, and achieves a speedup of over 5x in attention computation for long videos, surpassing state-of-the-art sparse attention methods at 90% sparsity. Code is available at https://github.com/EricLina/VMonarch.

articles.title: Shattered Compositionality: Counterintuitive Learning Dynamics of Transformers for Arithmetic
articles.summary:
arXiv:2601.22510v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often achieve strong benchmark accuracy yet remain brittle under small distribution shifts. While recent mechanistic studies reveal the discrepancy between LLMs and humans in skill compositions, the learning dynamics of skill acquisition and the role of data distributions remain elusive. In this study, we train transformers on synthetic arithmetic tasks with black-box model-agnostic metrics for analyzing non-human skill compositions. We discover that transformers often acquire skills for arithmetic in reverse order or in parallel instead of human-like sequential rules--a phenomenon we refer to as shattered compositionality. To explain these behaviors, we provide evidence that correlational matching to the training data, rather than causal or procedural composition, shapes learning dynamics. As a consequence, this non-human acquisition creates competition between partially learned skills, producing characteristic mixing errors and weaker robustness under controlled distribution shifts. We further show that the same qualitative behavior persists in modern LLMs and is not mitigated by pure model scaling or scratchpad supervision. Our results highlight a mismatch between training-time skill acquisition and the human-like hierarchical compositions, with implications for reasoning reliability and out-of-distribution robustness.

articles.title: Constrained Bilevel Reinforcement Learning via Approximate Lower-Level Responses
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.00282v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study constrained bilevel reinforcement learning in which the lower-level problem is a constrained Markov decision process with a generally parameterized policy. The lower-level solution map can be set-valued and need not be Lipschitz continuous in the upper-level variable, so standard hypergradient analyses do not apply. We therefore define the upper-level objective as the expected upper-level loss of the policy returned by a fixed stochastic lower-level algorithm, which we call the approximate response. This objective is well defined without uniqueness of the lower-level solution. To compute its gradient, we randomize the reward and constraint values used during lower-level training without changing their means, so that the upper-level variable affects training only through known probabilities. This yields an unbiased estimator of the upper-level objective's gradient that does not differentiate through the lower-level updates. We establish lower-level reward and feasibility guarantees, upper-level stationarity, and a total sample complexity of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\delta_\ell^{-6}\epsilon_o^{-2})$ over both levels, where $\delta_\ell$ is the lower-level accuracy and $\epsilon_o$ is the upper-level stationarity error. Setting $\delta_\ell=\epsilon_o=\epsilon$ gives $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-8})$.

articles.title: Learning-augmented smooth integer programs with PAC-learnable oracles
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.02505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We study an end-to-end learning-augmented framework for smooth integer programs, a broad class of Boolean polynomial optimization problems including MAX-CUT and MAX-k-SAT. An oracle learned from sampled instances predicts a full Boolean assignment for each unseen instance. For fixed-degree objectives, our polynomial-time pipeline, LEAP, linearizes the objective around the predicted assignment, solves an error-budgeted linear program, and rounds the fractional solution. We establish two guarantees. First, for any prediction, the approximation loss of LEAP degrades gracefully with prediction error: it is controlled by an error footprint that quantifies how much mispredicted coordinates can perturb the objective's local coefficients. Second, we bound the pseudo-dimension of the LEAP-induced cost class, yielding a PAC-style guarantee for learning an oracle from a predictor class via empirical risk minimization on instances from an unknown distribution. Together, these results give an end-to-end bound that separates the expected footprint loss of the best oracle in the class from the statistical error of learning. In experiments on MAX-CUT and MAX-SAT, LEAP substantially repairs imperfect predictions, empirical risk minimization selects effective oracle candidates, and the pipeline scales to application benchmarks with up to two million clauses.

articles.title: Joint Learning of Hierarchical Neural Options and Abstract World Model
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.02799v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Building agents that can perform new skills by composing existing skills is a long-standing goal of AI agent research. Towards this end, we investigate how to efficiently acquire a sequence of skills, formalized as hierarchical neural options. However, existing model-free hierarchical reinforcement algorithms need a lot of data. We propose a novel method, which we call AgentOWL (Option and World model Learning Agent), that jointly learns -- in a sample efficient way -- an abstract world model (abstracting across both states and time) and a set of hierarchical neural options. We show, on a subset of Object-Centric Atari games, that our method can learn more skills using less data than baseline methods and possesses learning and generalization capabilities that the baselines do not have.

articles.title: Learning pharmacokinetic dynamics with structured neural ODEs for precision dosing
articles.summary:
arXiv:2602.03215v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Individualized dosing requires predicting how a patient's drug exposure would change under a different dose or schedule. However, a model that accurately predicts exposure at the current dose may not reliably predict what happens when treatment changes.
